subtitle: a cereal that feeds itself nitrogen

effect: a guided enzyme cuts DNA at any spot spelled out by a short RNA
how: Making nitrogen fertiliser burns around one or two percent of the world's energy, and most of what is spread ends up in rivers rather than in the crop. Beans and clover avoid all of this by housing bacteria in root nodules that pull nitrogen from the air. Cereals have most of the signalling genes for building such nodules but do not switch them on; editing those switches, and pairing the seed with a matched bacterium, would let wheat make its own supply.
obstacle: Nodule building is a long conversation between plant and microbe, and no one has yet made a cereal hold up its end.
why: A famous unsolved goal; editing tools finally make the attempt tractable.
real: CRISPR-edited hexaploid wheat with raised apigenin exudation boosted free-living soil bacterial nitrogen fixation and yield under low fertiliser (UC Davis, Plant Biotechnology 2025) but deliberately avoids nodules, and nodulation-switch engineering in cereals (ENSA, a reported two-residue immunity-receptor edit enabling nodules in barley) remains unverified and undemonstrated as a nodulating wheat with a matched inoculant.
